title: Chapter 6 — Of The Relation Between Public Associations And Newspapers
paragraphs: When men are no longer bound to each other by firm and lasting ties, it is impossible to get the cooperation of any great number of them unless you can convince every man whose participation you need that his own private interest obliges him voluntarily to join his efforts to everyone else's. This can only be done regularly and conveniently by means of a newspaper. Nothing but a newspaper can drop the same thought into a thousand minds at the same moment. A newspaper is an adviser who does not need to be sought out but comes of his own accord and talks to you briefly, every day, about the common good, without pulling you away from your private affairs.

Newspapers therefore become more necessary as men become more equal and individualism grows more to be feared. To suppose they only serve to protect freedom would be to understate their importance: they sustain civilization. I will not deny that in democratic countries newspapers often lead citizens into badly thought-out schemes; but without newspapers there would be no common activity at all. The harm they do is therefore much less than the harm they cure.

The effect of a newspaper is not only to suggest the same purpose to a great many people; it also supplies the means for them to carry out together plans they may each have conceived singly. The leading citizens of an aristocratic country can see each other from far off, and if they wish to combine their forces, they move toward each other, drawing a crowd after them. In democratic countries, by contrast, it often happens that a great many men who would like or need to combine cannot, because being very minor and lost in the crowd, they cannot see one another and do not know where to find one another. A newspaper then takes up the idea or the feeling that had occurred to each of them at the same time but separately. All are at once drawn toward this beacon, and these wandering minds, which had long sought each other in the dark, at last meet and unite.

The newspaper brought them together, and the newspaper is still needed to keep them united. For an association among a democratic people to have any real power, it must be a numerous body. The people who make it up are therefore scattered over a wide area, and each of them is kept at home by the narrowness of his income or by the small unceasing efforts by which he earns it. A way must then be found for them to converse every day without seeing each other, and to act in common without having met. Hardly any democratic association can do without newspapers. There is therefore a necessary connection between public associations and newspapers: newspapers make associations, and associations make newspapers. And if it has been correctly said that associations will grow in number as the conditions of men become more equal, it is no less certain that the number of newspapers grows in proportion to the number of associations. That is why in America we find at the same time the greatest number of associations and of newspapers.

This connection between the number of newspapers and the number of associations leads us to another connection between the state of the periodical press and the form of administration in a country. It shows that the number of newspapers must diminish or increase in a democratic people in proportion as its administration is more or less centralized. For among democratic nations the exercise of local powers cannot be entrusted to the leading members of the community, as it is in aristocracies. Those powers must either be abolished or placed in the hands of very large numbers of men, who in fact then form an association permanently established by law to administer the affairs of a certain stretch of territory; and they need a journal to bring them each day, in the middle of their own minor concerns, some news of the state of their public affairs. The more local powers there are, the greater the number of men in whom they are vested by law; and since this need is felt constantly, the more abundantly newspapers multiply.

The extraordinary subdivision of administrative power has much more to do with the enormous number of American newspapers than does the country's great political freedom or the absolute liberty of its press. If all the inhabitants of the Union had the vote — but a vote only for the choice of their legislators in Congress — they would need only a few newspapers, because they would have to act together only on a few very important but very rare occasions. But within the large association of the nation, smaller associations have been established by law in every county, every city, and even every village, for the purposes of local administration. The laws of the country thus compel every American to cooperate every day of his life with some of his fellow citizens for a common purpose, and each of them needs a newspaper to tell him what all the others are doing.

I am of the opinion that a democratic people*a without any national representative assemblies but with a great number of small local powers would in the end have more newspapers than a people governed by a centralized administration and an elective legislature. What best explains to me the enormous circulation of the daily press in the United States is that I find among the Americans the greatest national freedom combined with local freedom of every kind. There is a prevailing opinion in France and England that the circulation of newspapers could be indefinitely increased by removing the taxes laid on the press. This is a very exaggerated estimate of the effects of such a reform. Newspapers multiply not in proportion to their cheapness, but in proportion to the more or less frequent need a great many people may feel to communicate with each other and to combine.

[Footnote a: I say a democratic people: the administration of an aristocratic people may be anything but centralized, and yet the need for newspapers may be little felt, because local powers are then held by a very small number of men who either act on their own or know one another and can easily meet and come to an understanding.]

In the same way I would attribute the growing influence of the daily press to causes more general than those usually cited. A newspaper can only survive on the condition that it publishes sentiments or principles held by a great many people. A newspaper therefore always represents an association made up of its regular readers. That association may be more or less defined, more or less narrow, more or less numerous; but the fact that the newspaper keeps going is proof that at least the germ of such an association exists in its readers' minds.

This leads me to one last reflection, with which I will close this chapter. The more equal the conditions of men become, and the less strong men are as individuals, the more easily they give way to the current of the multitude, and the harder it is for them to stand alone in holding an opinion that the multitude rejects. A newspaper represents an association. It may be said to address each of its readers in the name of all the others, and to exert its influence over them in proportion to their individual weakness. The power of the newspaper press must therefore grow as the social conditions of men become more equal.
